newsitem.title: ITALY: Right-winger Fini scores political triumph in Milan.
newsitem.headline: Right-winger Fini scores political triumph in Milan.

text.p: Italian hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini upstaged separatist Umberto Bossi on Sunday when he led at least 150,000 Italians through the streets of Milan in a carefully prepared march for unity.

Speaking in brilliant sunshine to a huge crowd packed into a main square in the north's biggest city, Fini savoured his moment of triumph at the end of a march which culminated in a tree-planting ceremony laden with symbols of Italian unity.

The big turnout for his post-fascist National Alliance party's rally was a slap in the face for Bossi, who has drawn only small crowds on a three-day trek across northern Italy to a planned proclamation of northern "independence" in Venice.

It was also an embarrassment for Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, which has scorned Bossi's calls for a "republic of Padania" but avoided holding rallies in support of national unity.
Speaking from a platform in front of an imposing mediaeval castle, Fini seized the opportunity to accuse Prodi of falling asleep while at the helm of the ship of state.
"The Prodi government is like the sleeping beauty," Fini told supporters gathered from all over the country, many of them waving the national red-white-and-green flag.
"It's not there and if it is, it's sleeping," added Fini, looking suntanned and dapper in a tailored suit.

"It's significant that only National Alliance felt the need to organise a rally like this, because in other countries the response to the secessionist delirium would have been organised by the government," he said.
Before speaking, Fini sang the national anthem with other party leaders. They were joined by former world middleweight boxing champion Nino Benvenuti and film comedian Lando Buzzanca.

A procession of right-wing mayors, many of them from the deep south of the country which Bossi's Northern League has frequently branded a burden to the nation, delivered patriotic messages to the crowd as they waited for Fini to speak.
By wrapping himself in the national flag, Fini made clear he was appealing to people of all political persuasions as a champion of the cause of national unity.
"This is a rally which the National Alliance dedicates to all Italians. Otherwise you cannot explain a turnout beyond all reasonable expectations," said Fini.

As thousands carrying flags and banners walked through the streets of Milan on the way to the rally, a Fini supporter with a loudhailer at the head of the march repeated the same patriotic slogan over and over again.
"What league? What secession? Italy, Italy is a single nation."
Not far behind a group of small children wearing coloured t-shirts with "I want to grow up Italian" printed across their chests chanted the slogan in unison.
Fini's National Alliance won 15.7 percent of votes to become Italy's third biggest party at the last general election in April and is part of the main opposition centre-right alliance.
Fini drew the biggest cheer when he said the only people in Europe favouring the break-up of Italy were Nazi-inspired Bavarians who dreamed of a Europe dominated by Germany.
He also appeared to strike a chord when he said it was time for the authorities to rein in Bossi after the secessionist firebrand called for the creation of a militia.
"We hope that from tomorrow in the event that enrollment (in the militia) begins, whoever is responsible for the respect of the democratic order steps in to repress a crime," he said.
